Last week's `library(tidyverse)` loads nine packages; today needs one function family from one of them ::: {{< vspace 1.5rem >}} # 1 · Data types [28 min]{.timing} ## 1.1 · The types, defined first (before any code) [5 min]{.timing} Every single value in R has a **type**. Here are the ones you'll live with, each with a Cal Poly example: | Type | What it is | Example value | |---|---|---| | **numeric** (double) | a number that can have decimals | `4.75` — a latte at Julian's | | **integer** | a whole number (written with an `L`) | `38L` — people in the Rec Center at 7 am | | **character** | text, in quotes | `"Scout Coffee"` | | **logical** | `TRUE` or `FALSE` | `TRUE` — the drink is iced | | **factor** | text from a *fixed menu* of allowed values | `"morning"` from {morning, afternoon, evening} | | **Date** / **date-time** | a calendar date; a date *and* clock time | `2026-09-22` / `2026-09-22 07:00:00` | | **NA** | a missing value — a hole, not a type of its own | the headcount nobody recorded | ::: {.callout-important title="Teaching note — definitions before class()"} - Read the table row by row *before* anyone runs code. The order today is: **define the type → then discover it with `class()`** - Ask: "If I write a latte price, which row?" (numeric) "The name of the shop?" (character) "Whether it's iced?" (logical) - `NA` gets one sentence: it's a placeholder for "nobody knows," and it can sit inside any type ::: ## 1.2 · Finding the type with `class()` [7 min]{.timing} **LM1 — `class()` tells you the type (4 min).** Predict each `class()` from the table above, *then* run: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # LM1: predict from the table, then run class(4.75) # Julian's latte ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "numeric" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} class(38L) # people in the Rec Center at 7 am ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "integer" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} class("Scout Coffee") # where the latte came from ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} class(TRUE) # iced? ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "logical" ``` ::: ::: > *Q1. Predictions: numeric · integer · character · logical* ::: {.callout-note title="Expected — LM1 & Q1"} - [LM1]{.lm} `"numeric"` · `"integer"` · `"character"` · `"logical"` - [Q1]{.q} most students predict `"numeric"` for `38L` — the `L` suffix is worth 30 seconds, no more: R stores whole numbers as integers when you ask, otherwise as doubles ::: **LM2 — doubles vs integers (1 min).** Both are numeric; `typeof()` tells them apart. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # LM2 typeof(4.75) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "double" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} typeof(38L) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "integer" ``` ::: ::: **LM3 — dates and date-times (2 min).** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # LM3 today <- Sys.Date() class(today) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Date" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} right_now <- Sys.time() class(right_now) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "POSIXct" "POSIXt" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note title="Expected — LM3"} - [LM3]{.lm} `"Date"` and `"POSIXct" "POSIXt"` - Say "date-time" and move on — lubridate handles the ugliness in week 4 ::: ## 1.3 · Three families: quantitative, categorical, other [6 min]{.timing} R's types sort into three families you'll use to pick plots and summaries all term: | Family | Question it answers | R types | Cal Poly examples | |---|---|---|---| | **Quantitative** | *how much? how many?* — you can average it | numeric, integer | latte price (`4.75`), Rec Center headcount (`38`), miles from campus (`2.3`) | | **Categorical** | *which kind? which group?* — you count it | character, factor, logical | coffee shop (`"Julian's"`, `"Starbucks"`, `"Scout"`), time slot (`"morning"`), iced (`TRUE`) | | **Other** (time/date) | *when?* — ordered, but not a plain number | Date, date-time | the day you bought the latte, the clock time you swiped into the Rec | ![The three families and, inside categorical, the character-vs-factor split. The dashed "Morning"? chip is the trap: a value not on a factor's menu becomes NA with no error.](/assets/types_families_map.svg){fig-alt="Three columns — quantitative (average it: numeric, integer), categorical (count it: character, factor, logical), other/time-date (Date, date-time) — each with Cal Poly examples and glimpse tags; below, a panel contrasting character (free text, four spellings of morning make four groups, alphabetical order) with factor (a fixed menu of levels in your order, where a value off the menu becomes NA silently)." width="100%"} > *Q2. Which family: (a) the number of people in the Rec Center at 5 pm · > (b) the shop that made your latte · (c) the date of the game vs. UCSB · > (d) whether you bought a latte today (yes/no)?* > > *Your answer:* (a) quantitative · (b) categorical · (c) other — a date · > (d) categorical — a logical is a two-level category. ::: {.callout-tip title="Q2 answer + why the families matter"} - [Q2]{.q} (a) **quantitative** (b) **categorical** (c) **other / date** (d) **categorical** — logical is a yes/no category - Why bother: quantitative → histograms and means; categorical → bar charts and counts; dates → line plots over time. Week 3's plots pick themselves once you name the family - Trap to name now: a number can be categorical. Your student ID is digits, but averaging student IDs is nonsense ::: **A small distinction — "string" vs "character".** Other languages call text a *string*. R calls the *type* **character**, and one piece of text (`"Scout Coffee"`) is a **string** — a character value of length one. So `"latte"` is a string, its class is character, and `c("latte", "mocha")` is a character *vector* of two strings. You'll hear both words; they are not in conflict. ## 1.4 · Factors vs characters — why it matters [6 min]{.timing} **LM4 — the same text, two types (4 min).** Rec Center headcounts come with a time slot. As character, the slots are just words; as a **factor**, they come with a fixed menu of allowed values (**levels**) *in an order you choose*: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # LM4: character vs factor slot_chr <- c("evening", "morning", "afternoon", "morning", "evening", "evening") slot_fct <- factor(slot_chr, levels = c("morning", "afternoon", "evening")) class(slot_chr) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} class(slot_fct) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "factor" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} levels(slot_fct) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "morning" "afternoon" "evening" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} table(slot_chr) # alphabetical — afternoon first ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` slot_chr afternoon evening morning 1 3 2 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} table(slot_fct) # the order YOU chose — morning first ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` slot_fct morning afternoon evening 2 1 3 ``` ::: ::: > 👀 **Variables check.** `slot_chr` and `slot_fct` are both listed — same six > values, but Variables describes one as *character* and one as *factor with > 3 levels*. That description IS the type. > *Q3. How many levels does `slot_fct` have, and what order did we give > them? Why would that order matter on a bar chart?* > > *Your answer:* 3 levels — morning, afternoon, evening. A bar chart follows > the levels, so the factor plots the day in time order; the character > version plots alphabetically (afternoon, evening, morning), which reads as > nonsense. ::: {.callout-tip title="Q3 answer — the two reasons factors exist"} - [Q3]{.q} **3 levels**, in the order morning → afternoon → evening - **Reason 1 — order.** Characters sort alphabetically; factors sort by *your* levels. Every plot and table of a categorical variable inherits that order - **Reason 2 — a fixed menu.** A factor knows `"night"` is *not* allowed (it becomes `NA`); a character column will happily accept `"Morning"`, `"morning "`, and `"AM"` as three different groups. Factors are how you catch typos in categories - Rule of thumb to leave them with: **character = free text (names, comments); factor = a category with a known set of values** - The menu metaphor pays rent in week 6 when forcats arrives ::: **LM5 — NA, the missing value (2 min).** `airquality` (built in) has real missing ozone readings; `is.na()` finds them and `sum()` counts them: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # LM5: count the missing values in Ozone sum(is.na(airquality$Ozone)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 37 ``` ::: ::: > *Q4. How many Ozone values are missing? 37* ::: {.callout-tip title="Q4 answer"} - [Q4]{.q} **37 missing** - First appearance of the `is.na()` + `sum()` idiom; students use it in every cycle ::: **LM6 — the is.\* family (2 min).** Test types with functions that return TRUE/FALSE: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # LM6: any correct fills work, e.g. is.numeric(4.75) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} is.character("Scout Coffee") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} is.logical(TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} is.factor(slot_fct) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: > *YT1 (4 min). ➕ Insert a chunk below. In it, find the `class()` of each of > the following, predicting first: `"TRUE"` (with quotes) · `4.75 > 4.25` · > `mtcars$cyl` · `Sys.Date() + 7`. Then in the comment, write which one > surprised you.* ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # YT1 — surprise: "TRUE" in quotes is character, and a comparison makes a logical class("TRUE") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} class(4.75 > 4.25) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "logical" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} class(mtcars$cyl) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "numeric" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} class(Sys.Date() + 7) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Date" ``` ::: ::: > *Predictions: character · logical · numeric · Date* ::: {.callout-note title="Expected — YT1"} - [YT1]{.yt} `"character"` · `"logical"` · `"numeric"` · `"Date"` - Surprise #1: `"TRUE"` — quotes make it text (a string!) - Surprise #2: `4.75 > 4.25` *produces* a logical — comparisons are how logicals get made in practice (`filter()` in two weeks) - `mtcars$cyl` being numeric though it only takes 4/6/8 previews activity item E: **the type R stores is not always the family the data means** ::: {{< vspace 1.5rem >}} # 2 · Data structures [24 min]{.timing} **LM7 — vector: one type, many values (4 min).** Built with `c()`. Three places to get a latte near campus: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # LM7: a vector shops <- c("Julian's", "Starbucks", "Scout Coffee") shops ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Julian's" "Starbucks" "Scout Coffee" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} length(shops) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} class(shops) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" ``` ::: ::: > *YT2 (4 min). ➕ Insert a chunk. What happens if you run `c(4.75, "five", 5.95)`? > Try it and look at the class.* ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # YT2 price <- c(4.75, 5.45, 5.95) size <- c("small", "medium", "large") iced <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE) price; size; iced ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4.75 5.45 5.95 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "small" "medium" "large" ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE FALSE TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} class(price); class(size); class(iced) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "numeric" ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "logical" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(4.75, "five", 5.95) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "4.75" "five" "5.95" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} class(c(4.75, "five", 5.95)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" ``` ::: ::: > *Q5. `c(4.75, "five", 5.95)` has class character. In one phrase, why?* > > *Your answer:* A vector holds one type, so R coerces everything to text. ::: {.callout-tip title="Q5 answer — coercion"} - [Q5]{.q} **character** - A vector holds *one* type, so R converts everything to the type that can hold all of it — text - This is **coercion**, arriving by accident rather than lecture — say the word once - They meet it again when a price column imports as `` because one row says "free" ::: **LM8 — data frame & tibble: vectors standing side by side (6 min).** Each column is a vector; every column has the same length. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # LM8: same data, two containers latte_df <- data.frame(shop = shops, price = c(4.75, 5.45, 5.95)) latte_tbl <- tibble(shop = shops, price = c(4.75, 5.45, 5.95)) latte_df ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # YT5c — error family: ____ factor(c("morning", "Morning", "evening"), levels = c("morning", "afternoon", "evening")) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # YT5c — error family: a value not on the factor's menu becomes NA (no error!) — "Morning" ≠ "morning" factor(c("morning", "morning", "evening"), levels = c("morning", "afternoon", "evening")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] morning morning evening Levels: morning afternoon evening ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-caution title="YT5 answers — three error families for types & structures"} - [YT5a]{.yt} `c(4.75, "5.45", 5.95)` → the vector is **character**; `mean()` warns *"argument is not numeric or logical: returning NA"* - family: **coercion** — one text value drags the whole vector to text.
